title: A hyperparameter heatmap asks: does the answer depend on the settings, or only on the problem?
summary: Each cell is one complete optimization run at one pair of settings, coloured by the final mean error. The picture is useful when the colours vary smoothly and the whole map spans little; it is misleading when a narrow range is stretched over the full colour bar or when single stochastic runs are read as structure.

media.alt: Heatmap with starting exponent p_start on the x axis (1, 2, 4, 5, 10) and final exponent p_final on the y axis (0.01 to 1), each cell coloured by mean relative error in percent with the value printed. Lighter cells lie toward the top rows, darker toward the bottom row, and the whole colour bar spans only a few percentage points.

source.caption: Hyperparameter sweep heatmap — n-heptane
source.note: A heatmap sweeping the power-mean objective's hyperparameters for n-heptane, showing which settings minimize error — generated from the accompanying sweep_summary.json.

read_the_figure.question: How much does the final fit quality change when the two annealing settings of the objective, the starting and final exponent, are changed?
read_the_figure.axes: x: starting exponent p_start (columns 1, 2, 4, 5, 10). y: final exponent p_final (nine rows from 0.01 to 1). Colour and the printed integer in each cell: the mean relative error (percent) reached by one run at those settings. The colour bar on the right fixes the scale; lighter yellow is lower error and dark purple is higher.
look_at: First read the colour bar, not the cells: note the lowest and highest value it spans. The span is only a few percentage points, so the full colour range is being used to show small differences.

Then look for a pattern across rows. A whole band of rows lighter than another band is a trend in p_final. A single light cell surrounded by darker neighbours is more likely run-to-run noise than a real optimum.
Compare the bottom row (p_final = 1, which is the classical average) with the top rows. This is the figure's central comparison: is the classical end of the sweep any better than the tuned end?
Compare columns. If colours barely change from left to right, the starting exponent does not matter much for this fuel.
Later heatmaps of this group print the value in each cell and name the solver in the caption. Check the solver before comparing two maps.
read_the_figure.proves: If the light cells form a contiguous region and the neighbouring cells agree with it, the chosen settings sit in a plateau: small changes in the settings do not change the answer much, so the result does not depend on a lucky choice. If instead the best cell is isolated, the sweep shows noise, not a recommendation.
if_wrong: Every cell the same colour: the objective is insensitive to both settings on this problem. The sweep then says nothing about which setting is best.
A checkerboard of light and dark cells: stochastic solver noise is larger than the effect of the settings. Replicate runs are needed before any cell can be called better.
Best cell on the edge of the grid: the optimum may lie outside the swept range, so the grid should be extended.
Printed integers look identical while the colours differ: rounding hides differences smaller than one unit. Trust the colour bar, but remember that those differences are small.
must_check: The colour bar has a stated unit and its range is shown; a data-driven range exaggerates small differences.
The colormap is perceptually ordered (a viridis-like one is), so lighter reliably means lower.
The number of runs behind each cell is stated. One run per cell cannot separate a setting effect from stochastic noise.
The solver is named (the heatmaps of this group come from more than one solver, and the caption of each says which).
The reference cell, here the classical setting p_final = 1, is easy to find.

terms.meaning: A setting of the method that is chosen before a run and is not fitted to the data, here the two exponents of the annealed objective.
A rule that moves a quantity from a starting value to a final value during the search. Here the exponent p starts at p_start and ends at p_final.
For positive numbers s_1..s_D, the generalized mean of exponent p. It is an ordinary average when p = 1, a geometric mean as p goes to 0, and it approaches the largest value as p grows.
Weighted mean relative error: a weighted average of relative errors over the target conditions. The legends in these figures call p = 1 the classical case.
Running the method once for every combination of a list of values per setting, then displaying a result per combination. Cost grows as the product of the list lengths.
An optimizer that uses random numbers (a genetic algorithm, CMA-ES). Two runs with identical settings can end at different values.
A colour scale whose lightness increases steadily with the value, so differences in brightness correspond to differences in the data.

remember: A heatmap cell is one run, not a law. For a stochastic solver, read it as a sample.
Read the colour bar first: the same colours can mean a 1 percent or a 100 percent range.
A plateau (many neighbouring cells equally good) is evidence of robustness; an isolated best cell is not.
p = 1 recovers the ordinary average, so the p_final = 1 row is the classical baseline inside the sweep.
Sweep cost is the product of the grid lengths times the number of replicates.

understand.title: Why a grid at all
understand.text: The two exponents interact: a high starting exponent changes how the early search weighs the worst conditions, and the final exponent sets what is optimized in the end. A grid shows every combination, so you can see interactions that two one-dimensional scans would hide.

understand.title: Why the range matters more than the colours
understand.text: A colormap always uses its full extent. A sweep whose errors differ by two or three percentage points looks as dramatic as one that differs by a factor of ten. The numbers on the colour bar, and the printed values in the cells, are what tell you the effect size.

understand.title: The other heatmaps of this group
understand.text: The same sweep is repeated for n-heptane, methyl butanoate and 1,3-butadiene, and later versions of the sweeps are resolved by solver: a covariance-matrix evolution strategy (CMA-ES) for two of the fuels and a genetic algorithm for the third, with the cell values printed. Reading them side by side asks one question: does the same region of the map stay good for different fuels and different solvers? Agreement is the evidence that the settings were not tuned to one data set.

steps.title: The power mean of a set of errors
steps.note: Standard definition. Raising to p before averaging changes how much each condition counts: a large p lets the largest errors dominate the average, a small p lets all conditions count more evenly.

steps.title: p = 1 is the ordinary average
steps.note: This is the classical mean of the errors. One condition with a very large error can supply most of the total.

steps.title: The limit p to 0 is the geometric mean
steps.note: Use e^x close to 1 + x for small p, then ln(1+x) close to x. So M_p tends to the geometric mean exp of the average log. Equal factors of improvement count equally, whichever condition they occur on.

steps.title: The limit p to infinity picks the worst case
steps.note: Factor out the largest s_d: M_p equals that value times (the fraction of terms near it, to the power p) to the 1/p, and the second factor tends to 1.

steps.title: Cost of the sweep
steps.note: This figure has five columns and nine rows, so 45 cells. With 10 replicates per cell the sweep would need 450 runs. This is why published sweeps usually have one run per cell, and why their cells must be read as noisy.

steps.title: Noise in one cell
steps.note: The standard error of a cell's mean falls as one over the square root of the number of replicates. To tell two cells apart, their difference must be several times this value.

steps.title: When a difference is worth reading
steps.note: A rough rule: a difference smaller than about two combined standard errors cannot be distinguished from noise.

worked.title: How many runs does the sweep cost, and what if replicated?
worked.problem: The heatmap has 5 values of p_start and 9 values of p_final. How many runs is one pass, and how many with 10 replicates per cell?

solution.text: One pass is one run per cell.

worked.answer: 45 runs for one pass and 450 with ten replicates per cell. Each stochastic cell in a one-pass map is therefore a single sample.

analyze.q: One cell in the middle of the map is clearly lighter than all its neighbours. Give two explanations and one extra run that separates them.
analyze.hint: Stochastic noise versus a real narrow optimum; repeat that cell with several seeds.

analyze.q: The bottom row is the classical setting. What does it mean for the story if the bottom row is the darkest band across all columns, and what would it mean if it were not?
analyze.hint: Think of the sweep as containing its own control.

analyze.q: Why can the same fuel look flat in one heatmap and structured in another that uses a different solver?
analyze.hint: A solver has its own noise and its own way of getting trapped in local minima.

evaluate.q: Would you recommend a single best cell from this figure? What would you want to see first?
evaluate.hint: Replicates, an agreement across fuels, and a plateau rather than a point.

evaluate.q: The colour bar spans only a few percentage points. Is a data-driven range honest here? What would you do instead?
evaluate.hint: Compare with a fixed range that includes the nominal and the classical errors, so the effect size is visible.

create: Redraw this figure as a heatmap plus a second panel showing the spread over replicate runs for each cell, using the same colour bar for both.
Design a sweep that keeps the cost below 100 runs but still tests whether the best region moves with the solver.

checks.q: What does one cell of the heatmap represent?
checks.answer: One complete optimization run at one pair of settings (p_start, p_final), coloured by the final mean relative error it reached.

checks.q: A sweep has 4 start values and 6 final values. How many runs are needed with 5 replicates per cell?
The lightest cell is isolated among darker cells. Is that evidence for a good setting?
checks.answer: Not by itself. An isolated light cell is the typical signature of run-to-run noise. A good region should show lighter neighbours too, or the cell should be reproduced with several seeds.

checks.q: The whole map spans about three percentage points in error. Is that a large or a small effect?
checks.hint: Compare with the nominal and classical errors elsewhere in the project.
checks.answer: Small compared with the improvement the method reports over the nominal mechanism, so the sweep supports 'not very sensitive to the settings', which is itself a useful result. Deciding more needs the replicate noise.

checks.q: How would you test that a chosen setting generalizes?
checks.answer: Run the same grid for other fuels or data sets and check that the same region stays good; a setting that is best on one data set only is overfitted to it.
